claim: Ancient genome sequencing technologies now provide the opportunity to study natural selection in unprecedented detail.
source: Ancient genome sequencing technologies now provide the opportunity to study natural selection in unprecedented detail.
evidence: This is a general statement about the capabilities of ancient genome sequencing technologies, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Methods for studying selection using ancient genomes often rely on partitioning individuals into discrete time periods or regions of the world.
source: Methods for studying selection using ancient genomes often rely on partitioning individuals into discrete time periods or regions of the world.
evidence: This describes current methodological approaches in the field, representing established knowledge about existing methods.

claim: The method introduced can handle time-stamped ancient samples, as well as genotype likelihoods and pseudohaploid sequences from low-coverage genomes.
source: Unlike previous approaches, our framework can handle time-stamped ancient samples, as well as genotype likelihoods and pseudohaploid sequences from low-coverage genomes.
evidence: This is a claim about the capabilities of the method developed in this study, supported by the methodological description in the manuscript.

claim: The method was applied to a panel of published ancient West Eurasian genomes to produce dynamic maps showcasing the inferred spread of candidate beneficial alleles over time and space.
source: We apply the method to a panel of published ancient West Eurasian genomes to produce dynamic maps showcasing the inferred spread of candidate beneficial alleles over time and space.
evidence: This describes the application of the method to real data, as demonstrated in the Results section with figures showing allele frequency dynamics.

claim: The method provides estimates for the strength of selection and diffusion rate for each analyzed allele.
source: We also provide estimates for the strength of selection and diffusion rate for each of these alleles.
evidence: This is supported by the parameter estimates presented in the Results section and appendix tables.

claim: The problem of estimating the age of a beneficial allele has yielded a rich methodological literature.
source: The problem of estimating the age of a beneficial allele, for example, has yielded a rich methodological literature (Slatkin and Rannala, 2000), and recent methods have exploited fine-scale haplotype information to produce highly accurate age estimates (Mathieson and McVean, 2014; Platt et al., 2019; Albers and McVean, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple published works on allele age estimation methods.

claim: Recent methods have exploited fine-scale haplotype information to produce highly accurate age estimates.
source: The problem of estimating the age of a beneficial allele, for example, has yielded a rich methodological literature (Slatkin and Rannala, 2000), and recent methods have exploited fine-scale haplotype information to produce highly accurate age estimates (Mathieson and McVean, 2014; Platt et al., 2019; Albers and McVean, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific methodological papers.

claim: Efforts to infer the geographic origins of beneficial mutations are scarcer than efforts to estimate allele age.
source: In contrast, efforts to infer the geographic origins of beneficial mutations are scarcer.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the state of the field, based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Novembre et al., 2005 developed a maximum likelihood method to model the origin and spread of a beneficial mutation.
source: These include Novembre et al., 2005, who developed a maximum likelihood method to model the origin and spread of a beneficial mutation and applied it to the CCR5-Δ32 allele, which was, at the time, considered to have been under positive selection (Stephens et al., 1998; Sabeti et al., 2005; Novembre and Han, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the Novembre et al., 2005 paper.

claim: Itan et al., 2009 developed an approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) approach using demic simulations to find the geographic and temporal origins of a beneficial allele.
source: Similarly, Itan et al., 2009 developed an approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) approach using demic simulations, in order to find the geographic and temporal origins of a beneficial allele, based on present-day allele frequency patterns.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the Itan et al., 2009 paper.

claim: Ancient genomes are increasingly being used to understand the process of natural selection.
source: As ancient genome sequences become more readily available, they are increasingly being used to understand the process of natural selection (see reviews in Malaspinas et al., 2012; Dehasque et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review papers on the topic.

claim: Few studies have used ancient genomes to fit spatial dynamic models of the spread of an allele over a landscape.
source: However, few studies have used ancient genomes to fit spatial dynamic models of the spread of an allele over a landscape.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Most spatiotemporal analyses that included ancient genomes have used descriptive modeling to learn the spatiotemporal covariance structure of allele frequencies or hidden ancestry clusters.
source: Most spatiotemporal analyses that included ancient genomes have used descriptive modeling in order to learn the spatiotemporal covariance structure of allele frequencies (Segurel et al., 2020) or hidden ancestry clusters (Racimo et al., 2020b), and then used that structure to hindcast these patterns onto a continuous temporally evolving landscape.
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies using descriptive modeling approaches.

claim: Dynamic models have the power to infer interpretable parameters from genomic data and perhaps reveal the ultimate causes for observed patterns.
source: In contrast to descriptive approaches, dynamic models have the power to infer interpretable parameters from genomic data and perhaps reveal the ultimate causes for these patterns (Wikle et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a general statement about the advantages of dynamic models, supported by a citation.

claim: The geographic origin of the rs4988235(T) allele remains elusive.
source: For example, the geographic origin of the rs4988235(T) allele—upstream of the LCT gene and associated with adult lactase persistence in most of Western Eurasia (Enattah et al., 2002)—remains elusive, as is the way in which it spread (an extensive review can be found in Ségurel and Bon, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review paper on the topic.

claim: The rs4988235(T) allele is upstream of the LCT gene and associated with adult lactase persistence in most of Western Eurasia.
source: For example, the geographic origin of the rs4988235(T) allele—upstream of the LCT gene and associated with adult lactase persistence in most of Western Eurasia (Enattah et al., 2002)—remains elusive, as is the way in which it spread (an extensive review can be found in Ségurel and Bon, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Enattah et al., 2002.

claim: The rs4988235(T) allele has been found in different populations with frequencies ranging from 5% up to almost 100%.
source: The allele has been found in different populations, with frequencies ranging from 5% up to almost 100%, and its selection coefficient has been estimated to be among the highest in human populations (Bersaglieri et al., 2004; Enattah et al., 2008; Tishkoff et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies documenting allele frequencies.

claim: The selection coefficient of the rs4988235(T) allele has been estimated to be among the highest in human populations.
source: The allele has been found in different populations, with frequencies ranging from 5% up to almost 100%, and its selection coefficient has been estimated to be among the highest in human populations (Bersaglieri et al., 2004; Enattah et al., 2008; Tishkoff et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies estimating selection coefficients.

claim: The exact causes for the adaptive advantage of the rs4988235(T) allele are contested.
source: However, the exact causes for its adaptive advantage are contested (Szpak et al., 2019), and it has been suggested that the selection pressures acting on the allele may have been different in different parts of the continent (Gerbault et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers discussing the adaptive advantage.

claim: It has been suggested that the selection pressures acting on the rs4988235(T) allele may have been different in different parts of the continent.
source: However, the exact causes for its adaptive advantage are contested (Szpak et al., 2019), and it has been suggested that the selection pressures acting on the allele may have been different in different parts of the continent (Gerbault et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gerbault et al., 2009.

claim: Ancient DNA evidence shows that the rs4988235(T) allele was rare in Europe during the Neolithic.
source: Ancient DNA evidence shows that the allele was rare in Europe during the Neolithic (Burger et al., 2007; Gamba et al., 2014; Allentoft et al., 2015; Mathieson et al., 2015) and only became common in Northern Europe after the Iron Age, suggesting a rise in frequency during this period, perhaps mediated by gene flow from regions east of the Baltic where this allele was more common during the onset of the Bronze Age (Krüttli et al., 2014; Margaryan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple ancient DNA studies.

claim: The rs4988235(T) allele only became common in Northern Europe after the Iron Age.
source: Ancient DNA evidence shows that the allele was rare in Europe during the Neolithic (Burger et al., 2007; Gamba et al., 2014; Allentoft et al., 2015; Mathieson et al., 2015) and only became common in Northern Europe after the Iron Age, suggesting a rise in frequency during this period, perhaps mediated by gene flow from regions east of the Baltic where this allele was more common during the onset of the Bronze Age (Krüttli et al., 2014; Margaryan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to ancient DNA studies.

claim: Itan et al., 2009 estimated that the rs4988235(T) allele was first under selection among farmers around 7500 years ago possibly between the Central Balkans and Central Europe.
source: Itan et al., 2009 deployed their ABC approach to model the spatial spread of the rs4988235(T) allele and estimated that it was first under selection among farmers around 7500 years ago possibly between the Central Balkans and Central Europe.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Itan et al., 2009.

claim: Others have postulated a steppe origin for the rs4988235(T) allele.
source: Others have postulated a steppe origin for the allele (Allentoft et al., 2015), given that the rise in frequency appears to have occurred during and after the Bronze Age migration of steppe peoples into Western Eurasia (Haak et al., 2015; Allentoft et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies proposing a steppe origin.

claim: The rs4988235(T) allele is at low frequency in genomes of Bronze Age individuals associated with Corded Ware and Bell Beaker assemblages in Central Europe who have high steppe ancestry.
source: However, the allele is at low frequency in genomes of Bronze Age individuals associated with Corded Ware and Bell Beaker assemblages in Central Europe who have high steppe ancestry (Mathieson et al., 2015; Margaryan et al., 2020), complicating the story further (Ségurel and Bon, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to ancient DNA studies.

claim: The origins and spread dynamics of large-effect pigmentation-associated SNPs in ancient Eurasians have been intensely studied.
source: The origins and spread dynamics of large-effect pigmentation-associated SNPs in ancient Eurasians have also been intensely studied (Ju and Mathieson, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review paper.

claim: Major loci of large effect on skin, eye, and hair pigmentation have been documented as having been under recent positive selection in Western Eurasian history.
source: Major loci of large effect on skin, eye, and hair pigmentation have been documented as having been under recent positive selection in Western Eurasian history (Voight et al., 2006; Sabeti et al., 2007; Pickrell et al., 2009; Lao et al., 2007; Mathieson et al., 2015; Alonso et al., 2008; Hudjashov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies documenting selection on pigmentation loci.

claim: Genes SLC45A2, OCA2, HERC2, SLC24A5, and TYR include loci of large effect on pigmentation that have been under recent positive selection.
source: These include genes SLC45A2, OCA2, HERC2, SLC24A5, and TYR.
evidence: This follows from the previous statement about pigmentation loci under selection.

claim: Selection at the TYR locus is thought to have occurred particularly recently, over the last 5000 years.
source: Among these, selection at the TYR locus is thought to have occurred particularly recently, over the last 5000 years (Stern et al., 2019), driven by a recent mutation (Albers and McVean, 2020) that may have spread rapidly in Western Eurasia.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on TYR selection timing.

claim: Selection at the TYR locus was driven by a recent mutation.
source: Among these, selection at the TYR locus is thought to have occurred particularly recently, over the last 5000 years (Stern et al., 2019), driven by a recent mutation (Albers and McVean, 2020) that may have spread rapidly in Western Eurasia.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Albers and McVean, 2020.

claim: The method is based on a model proposed by Novembre et al., 2005 to fit allele frequencies in two dimensions to present-day genotype data spread over a densely sampled map.
source: We based our statistical inference framework on a model proposed by Novembre et al., 2005 to fit allele frequencies in two dimensions to present-day genotype data spread over a densely sampled map.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Novembre et al., 2005 and describes the methodological foundation.

claim: Model C includes two advection terms (vx and vy), allowing the center of mass of the allele's frequency to diverge from its origin over time.
source: Finally, model C is even more general and includes two advection terms (vx and vy), allowing the center of mass of the allele's frequency to diverge from its origin over time.
evidence: This describes the parameters of model C as presented in the Methods section.

claim: The incorporation of advection is meant to account for the fact that population displacements and expansions could have led to allele frequency dynamics that are poorly explained by diffusion alone.
source: The incorporation of advection is meant to account for the fact that population displacements and expansions could have led to allele frequency dynamics that are poorly explained by diffusion alone.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement explaining the motivation for including advection terms in the model.

claim: Previously published allele age estimates were used from a nonparametric approach leveraging patterns of haplotype concordance and discordance around the mutation of interest.
source: In order to establish a starting time point for our diffusion process, we used previously published allele age estimates obtained from a nonparametric approach leveraging the patterns of haplotype concordance and discordance around the mutation of interest (Albers and McVean, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Albers and McVean, 2020.

claim: For the LCT/MCM6 region allele, age estimates based on an approximate Bayesian computation approach were also used.
source: In the case of the allele in the LCT/MCM6 region, we also used age estimates based on an approximate Bayesian computation approach (Itan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Itan et al., 2009.

claim: The model is more accurate at correctly inferring the parameters for the time period before 5000 years BP.
source: Overall, the model is more accurate at correctly inferring the parameters for the time period before 5000 years BP (Figure 1b), with decreased performance when longitudinal diffusion is high (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The model has decreased performance when longitudinal diffusion is high.
source: Overall, the model is more accurate at correctly inferring the parameters for the time period before 5000 years BP (Figure 1b), with decreased performance when longitudinal diffusion is high (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The method is generally able to estimate the selection coefficient accurately in simulations including advection.
source: We found that our method is generally able to estimate the selection coefficient accurately.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results for model C presented in the Results section.

claim: In some simulations, discrepancies were found between the estimated and true diffusion and advection coefficients, often occurring because of a misestimated origin forcing the other parameters to adjust.
source: However, in some of the simulations, we found discrepancies between the estimated and true diffusion and advection coefficients, often occurring because of a misestimated origin forcing the other parameters to adjust in order to better fit the allele frequency distribution in later stages of the allele's spread (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Different combinations of parameters can produce similar present-day allele frequency distributions.
source: Despite the disparities between the true and inferred parameter values, the resulting surface plots become very similar as we approach the present, suggesting that different combinations of parameters can produce similar present-day allele frequency distributions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results comparing true and inferred allele frequency maps.

claim: When model C (including advection) is applied to simulations generated without advection, the advection coefficients are inferred to be non-zero.
source: We can observe that the advection coefficients are inferred to be non-zero (Figure 1—figure supplements 6b and 7b); however, the inferred allele frequency dynamic plots closely resemble the ones obtained with true parameter values (Figure 1—figure supplements 6a and 7a).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 6 and 7.

claim: Complex interactions between the diffusion and advection coefficients can result in similar outcomes even when only diffusion is considered in the model.
source: This shows that complex interactions between the diffusion and advection coefficients can result in similar outcomes even when only diffusion is considered in the model.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results comparing models with and without advection.

claim: The selection coefficient estimates are inferred highly accurately regardless of the sampling scheme chosen.
source: The selection coefficient estimates are inferred highly accurately, regardless of the sampling scheme chosen, and lie close to the true value, with only a slight underestimation in the time period after 5000 years BP (with the exception of the 'extreme 25%/75%').
evidence: This is supported by the sampling scheme simulation results summarized in Appendix 2—table 3.

claim: The origin of the allele inferred by the model closely corresponds to the first observation of the derived allele in the individual-based simulation.
source: We can see that the origin of the allele inferred by the model closely corresponds to the first observation of the derived allele in the simulation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the individual-based simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The inferred selection coefficient from the individual-based simulation is only slightly higher than the true value (0.0366 vs. 0.030).
source: The inferred selection coefficient is only slightly higher than the true value from the simulation (0.0366 vs. 0.030).
evidence: This is supported by the individual-based simulation results.

claim: A two-period scheme was used by allowing the model to have two sets of estimates for the selection coefficient and the diffusion and advection coefficients in two different periods of time: before and after 5000 years ago.
source: We used a two-period scheme by allowing the model to have two sets of estimates for the selection coefficient and the diffusion and advection coefficients in two different periods of time: before and after 5000 years ago, reflecting the change in population dynamics and mobility before and after the Bronze Age transition (Loog et al., 2017; Racimo et al., 2020a).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the analysis, supported by citations explaining the rationale.

claim: The two-period scheme reflects the change in population dynamics and mobility before and after the Bronze Age transition.
source: We used a two-period scheme by allowing the model to have two sets of estimates for the selection coefficient and the diffusion and advection coefficients in two different periods of time: before and after 5000 years ago, reflecting the change in population dynamics and mobility before and after the Bronze Age transition (Loog et al., 2017; Racimo et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies documenting Bronze Age population changes.

claim: Assuming the mutation age estimate is equivalent to the start of selection onset from Itan et al., 2009, the origin of the rs4988235(T) allele is estimated to be north of the Caucasus, around what is now southwestern Russia and eastern Ukraine.
source: Assuming the mutation age estimate is equivalent to the start of selection onset from Itan et al., 2009, the origin of the allele is estimated to be north of the Caucasus, around what is now southwestern Russia and eastern Ukraine (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis results shown in Figure 6b.

claim: A net westward advection parameter is estimated for rs4988235(T), indicating movement of the allele frequency's center of mass to the west as we approach the present.
source: We also estimate stronger diffusion in the second period than in the first, to accommodate the rapid expansion of the allele throughout Western Europe, and a net westward advection parameter, indicating movement of the allele frequency's center of mass to the west as we approach the present.
evidence: This is supported by the parameter estimates presented in Appendix 2—table 5.

claim: Assuming the older age estimate from Albers and McVean, 2020, the origin of the rs4988235(T) allele is estimated to be in the northeast of Europe.
source: Assuming the older age estimate from Albers and McVean, 2020, the origin of the allele is estimated to be in the northeast of Europe (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), which is at a much higher latitude than the first occurrence of the allele, in Ukraine.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The estimated selection coefficients for rs1042602(A) are 0.0221 (95% CI: 0.0216–0.0227) and 0.0102 (95% CI: 0.0083–0.0120) for the time periods before and after 5000 years BP, respectively.
source: In the case of the rs1042602(A) allele, our estimated selection coefficients of 0.0221 (95% CI: 0.0216–0.0227) and 0.0102 (95% CI: 0.0083–0.0120) for the time periods before and after 5000 years BP, respectively, are generally in agreement with previous results.
evidence: This is supported by the parameter estimates presented in Appendix 2—table 7.

claim: Wilde et al., 2014 used a forward simulation approach to infer a point estimate of 0.026 for the selection coefficient at rs1042602.
source: Wilde et al., 2014 used a forward simulation approach to infer a point estimate of 0.026.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wilde et al., 2014.

claim: Nakagome et al., 2019 estimated the strength of selection acting on rs1042602 to be 0.013 (0.002–0.029) using an approximate Bayesian computation framework.
source: Another study using an approximate Bayesian computation framework (Nakagome et al., 2019) estimated the strength of selection acting on rs1042602 to be 0.013 (0.002–0.029).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nakagome et al., 2019.

claim: The estimates of the longitudinal advection parameter are negative for both the SNPs in the TYR and LCT loci.
source: Our estimates of the longitudinal advection parameter are negative for both the SNPs in the TYR and LCT loci: the mutation origins are always to the east of the center of mass of the allele frequency distribution seen in present-day data.
evidence: This is supported by the parameter estimates presented in the appendix tables.

claim: The negative longitudinal advection parameter perhaps reflects common migratory processes, like the large-scale Neolithic and Bronze Age population movements from east to west.
source: This perhaps reflects common migratory processes, like the large-scale Neolithic and Bronze Age population movements from east to west, affecting the allele frequencies at these loci across the Eurasian landscape (Allentoft et al., 2015; Haak et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to studies documenting east-to-west migrations.

claim: When allowing for advection, the inferred location of the allele origin tends to become less accurate.
source: However, when allowing for advection, the inferred location tends to become less accurate.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results comparing models with and without advection.

claim: Migration events early in the dispersal of the selected allele could create difficulties in finding the true allele origin if net directional movement had a large effect in this dispersal.
source: This suggests that migration events early in the dispersal of the selected allele could create difficulties in finding the true allele origin if net directional movement (i.e., via major migratory processes) had a large effect in this dispersal.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results and methodological limitations.

claim: The issue of inaccurate origin inference could be alleviated with the inclusion of more ancient genomes around the time of the origin of the mutation.
source: This issue could be alleviated with the inclusion of more ancient genomes around the time of the origin of the mutation, perhaps in combination with a more fine-scaled division into periods where advection may have occurred in different directions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential improvements to the method.

claim: Various studies have estimated the selection coefficient for the rs4988235(T) allele, ranging from as low as 0.014 to as high as 0.19.
source: Various studies have estimated the selection coefficient for the rs4988235(T) allele, and these range from as low as 0.014 to as high as 0.19 (Enattah et al., 2008; Mathieson and Mathieson, 2018; Mathieson, 2020; Stern et al., 2019; Burger et al., 2020; Peter et al., 2012; Gerbault et al., 2009; Itan et al., 2009; Bersaglieri et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies estimating selection coefficients.

claim: Recent papers incorporating ancient DNA estimate the selection coefficient for rs4988235(T) to be as low as 0 (in certain regions of Southern Europe) and as high as 0.06.
source: Recent papers incorporating ancient DNA estimate the selection coefficient to be as low as 0 (in certain regions of Southern Europe) and as high as 0.06 (Mathieson and Mathieson, 2018; Mathieson, 2020; Burger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent ancient DNA studies.

claim: It is likely that the selection coefficient for rs4988235(T) was different for different regions of Europe, perhaps due to varying cultural practices.
source: It is also likely that the selection coefficient was different for different regions of Europe, perhaps due to varying cultural practices (Mathieson, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mathieson, 2020.

claim: The estimated selection coefficient for rs4988235(T) during the first period depends strongly on the assumed allele age (s = 0.0993 vs. s = 0.0285).
source: In our case, the estimated selection coefficient during the first period—before 5000 years ago—depends strongly on the assumed allele age (s = 0.0993 vs. s = 0.0285).
evidence: This is supported by the parameter estimates presented in Appendix 2—tables 5 and 6.

claim: The estimates for the selection coefficient of rs4988235(T) in the second period are more robust to the assumed age: s = 0.0328 (95% CI: 0.0327–0.0329) if assuming the younger allele age and s = 0.0255 (95% CI: 0.0252–0.0258) if assuming the older allele age.
source: The estimates for the second period—after 5000 years ago—are more robust to the assumed age: s = 0.0328 (95% CI: 0.0327–0.0329) if we assume the younger allele age (7441 years ago) and s = 0.0255 (95% CI: 0.0252–0.0258) if we assume the older allele age (20,106 years ago).
evidence: This is supported by the parameter estimates presented in Appendix 2—tables 5 and 6.

claim: The selection coefficient estimates for rs4988235(T) in the second period are within the range of previous estimates.
source: These estimates are also within the range of previous estimates.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the current results to previously published estimates.

claim: When investigating the robustness of the geographic origin of both rs4988235(T) and rs1042602(A), parameters related to the beneficial allele's expansion change in response to different assumed origins of the allele.
source: When investigating the robustness of the geographic origin of both rs4988235(T) and rs1042602(A), we found that parameters related to the beneficial allele's expansion change in response to different assumed origins of the allele.
evidence: This is supported by the robustness analysis results presented in the appendix tables.

claim: The resulting allele frequency surface plots appear very similar throughout the later stages of the process regardless of the assumed origin.
source: The resulting allele frequency surface plots, however, appear very similar throughout the later stages of the process, showing that the model tends to adjust the diffusion and advection coefficients in a way such that the allele will end up expanding into the same areas regardless of the origin.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the robustness analysis results.

claim: The assumptions of spatiotemporal homogeneity of the parameters seem less plausible when applying these methods to longer time scales and broader geographic areas.
source: As we apply these methods to longer time scales and broader geographic areas, the assumptions of spatiotemporal homogeneity of the parameters seem less plausible.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement about the limitations of the model assumptions.

claim: The results for the spread of the rs4988235(T) allele during the older time period should be interpreted with caution, since they may be affected by sparse sampling in the early Holocene.
source: Notably, our results for the spread of the rs4988235(T) allele during the older time period should be interpreted with caution, since they may be affected by sparse sampling in the early Holocene.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the limitations of the data and results.

claim: Potential future extensions of the method could incorporate geographic features and historical migration events that create spatially or temporally varying moderators of gene flow.
source: Potential future extensions of our method could incorporate geographic features and historical migration events that create spatially or temporally varying moderators of gene flow.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential improvements to the method.

claim: The retreat of glaciers after the last Glacial maximum allowed migration of humans into Scandinavia.
source: An example of this type of processes is the retreat of glaciers after the last Glacial maximum, which allowed migration of humans into Scandinavia (Günther et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Günther et al., 2018.

claim: The model only accounts for diffusion in two directions.
source: As described above, our model only accounts for diffusion in two directions.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the current model.

claim: Further extension of the model could incorporate anisotropic diffusion.
source: Further extension of our model could therefore incorporate anisotropic diffusion (Othmer et al., 1988; Painter and Hillen, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential improvements, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Another possibility could be the introduction of stochastic process components to convert the partial differential equations into stochastic differential equations.
source: Another possibility could be the introduction of stochastic process components in order to convert the partial differential equations into stochastic differential equations (Brown et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential improvements, supported by a citation.

claim: Stochastic components could serve to induce spatial autocorrelation and capture local patterns of allele frequency covariance in space.
source: Stochastic components could serve to induce spatial autocorrelation and capture local patterns of allele frequency covariance in space that might not be well modeled by the deterministic partial differential equations (PDEs) (Cressie and Wikle, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential improvements, supported by a citation.

claim: Stochastic components could serve to induce stochasticity in allele frequency changes over time as a consequence of genetic drift.
source: They could also serve to induce stochasticity in allele frequency changes over time as a consequence of genetic drift (Crow and Kimura, 1970), allowing one to model the dynamics of more weakly selected variants, where drift plays an important role.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential improvements, supported by a citation.

claim: One could perhaps combine information across loci to jointly model the spatiotemporal frequency surfaces at multiple loci associated with the same trait.
source: Eventually, one could perhaps combine information across loci to jointly model the spatiotemporal frequency surfaces at multiple loci associated with the same trait.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.

claim: The availability of hundreds of ancient genomes and the increasing interest in spatiotemporal method development will likely lead researchers to posit new questions and hypotheses about the behavior of natural selection.
source: The availability of hundreds of ancient genomes (Marciniak and Perry, 2017) and the increasing interest in spatiotemporal method development (Bradburd and Ralph, 2019), such as the one described in this article, will likely lead researchers to posit new questions and hypotheses about the behavior of natural selection.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions, supported by citations.

claim: There is a lack of vocabulary for distinguishing between different spatiotemporal scenarios of selection.
source: In contrast, there is a lack of vocabulary for distinguishing between a scenario of strong selection that is locally constrained in space from a scenario of widespread selection extended over a landscape, or a model of neutral diffusion in space followed by parallel non-neutral increases in frequency at multiple locations.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of terminology in the field.

claim: Ralph and Coop, 2010 showed how multiple localized hard sweeps may be seen as a soft sweep at a larger population-wide scale.
source: For example, Ralph and Coop, 2010 showed how multiple localized hard sweeps may be seen as a soft sweep at a larger population-wide scale.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ralph and Coop, 2010.

claim: Population genetic models that explicitly account for space and time are an important area of future methodological development.
source: Population genetic models that explicitly account for space and time are an important area of future methodological development (Bradburd and Ralph, 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions, supported by a citation.

claim: Spatiotemporal information can greatly help improve our knowledge of how natural selection operated in the past.
